blocks.text: …panic is not helpful

Conflicts are a normal part of our dogs’ social lives and indispensable for stable social competence in future. However, they are only beneficial if they do not harm the dog and instead bring learning experiences.
Whether problematic conflicts occur and how they develop depends to a high degree on the quality of our leadership.
The most important step for avoiding problematic conflicts: CREATE DISTANCE! – trained daily as a fixed routine in everyday life.
What you should know 📋
To avoid the risk of conflict between dogs, the rule always applies: train together with other dogs as often as possible.
The way we react in conflict situations has a decisive share in the course, effect and outcome of events.
Conflict situations that arise from human error or a misjudgement of the situation are to be classed as highly problematic and must be avoided at all costs.

The three training situations – on leash, off leash, several dogs – build on one another. We always begin with Case 1 and only move up to the next level when the current one is secure and consolidated in everyday life.
Warning signals – reading the dog early 👁️

Successful de-escalation begins before the actual situation arises. Through subtle body language, our dog shows that it has noticed another dog: increased body tension, frozen gaze, ears forward, slowed steps, head or tail slightly raised.
These warning signals are our starting signal – not barking, pulling or fixating. Anyone who reacts to the early signals has considerably more time, space and calm available.
We consciously train our perception: the dog’s body tension and direction of gaze often tell us more than what we ourselves already see.
Training 🦮

When we notice an encounter situation developing, we calmly, composedly and wordlessly – or at the very least speaking calmly – take an alternative direction with our dog that leads us away from the other dog in a neutral direction.

Even where space is limited, the maximum possible distance should be created. The leash must on no account be shortened more than necessary. The longer the leash is left, the less our dog enters a state of tension.
At the earliest once our dog comes along reasonably willingly, within the limits of what is possible, we stand still calmly and bring it into “sit” or “down”.
In the sense of lasting, positive learning, the process is only complete when our dog holds the position and does not have to be actively held there by us.
Finally – after the other dog is out of perception – we bring our dog from “down” into “sit” if necessary, praise it extensively, gladly confirm with a short game and calmly continue on our way.
Actively seeking and assessing the safe place 📍
The “safe place” is a deliberately chosen position: sufficient distance from the source of the stimulus, visual cover if possible, no dead end, enough room for us and the dog.
Ideal positions are: areas set back to the side, driveways or wider verges, green areas with natural visual cover from bushes or trees.
We train ourselves to actively look for these places as soon as we recognise the warning signals – not only once things have escalated. Anyone who plans ahead always has a good option.
Important: A safe place loses its value if we go to it too late. The quality of the place and the timing of going to it together decide the training success.
Effect ✅
Over time, our dog learns that it is very worthwhile for it to seek out distance instead of entering the conflict – because safety, low stress and a subsequent game with us are waiting there.
In the course of the sequences, we may present the toy or the food bag as early as when leaving the situation, in order to win our dog over to us immediately.
However, as a matter of principle, we only praise or play after the other dog has left the stage.
What we remember 🧠
Recognise the dog’s warning signals early and react immediately.
Recognise the situation early – the leash stays as long as possible.
Leave the situation far enough – bring the dog into “sit” or “down” at the safe, deliberately chosen place.
Wait – if necessary improve the position once more.
After the other party has gone, praise extensively and play.
Sources of error ⚠️
A leash held short and thus permanently taut puts our dog into a high state of tension and thus into unwanted behaviour.
Going to the safe place too late causes the situation to escalate – the learning effect turns negative.
By reacting in a hectic, hesitant, loud and emotional way, we convey a state of alarm to our dog, which it immediately acts out with unwanted behaviour.
Step-by-step plan – from calm to urban 📈
Level 1 – Familiar, quiet surroundings: We first train the recall from encounter situations on familiar, quiet areas. This is where the dog’s basic trust in the sequence develops.
Level 2 – Unfamiliar surroundings, little activity: New places with moderate stimulation. Our dog learns that the recall applies regardless of location.
Level 3 – Urban surroundings, controlled encounters: Only once Levels 1 and 2 are secure do we go into the city. Anticipation counts here: recognise situations early, recall calmly, lead out safely.
Anyone who skips the levels risks that the dog does not know the recall as a reliable sequence when things escalate – precisely when we need it most.
Training 🦮

When we notice an encounter situation developing, we bring our dog into a controllable state with “down” – or at least with “sit” – and then call it smoothly and briskly along with us in a neutral direction away.
We immediately walk out of the situation without interruption until we have reached a distance that allows us to bring the dog into “down” without problems.

If the situation develops unpredictably, an immediate “down” or “sit” can save the situation – we then use the opportunity to approach the dog inconspicuously but quickly, put it on the leash and lead it out of the situation as in Case 1.

A strict prerequisite is sufficiently consolidated training of off-leash work. A successful resolution necessarily requires that dog and dog handler are well trained and consolidated in everyday life with regard to “down”, “sit” and off-leash work.
Reducing our own agitation – before the recall 🧘
One of the most common sources of error in the off-leash recall is our own tension. Our dog reads it immediately – and interprets it as confirmation that the situation really is dangerous.

A simple, effective technique: when recognising the situation, consciously breathe out once, deeply and calmly, before we give the first command. This one breath gives us back a moment of control and lowers body tension – which the dog feels immediately.
Over time this inner sequence becomes routine: recognise the situation – briefly breathe out – recall calmly – lead out briskly.
Training the recall as a reward event 🌟
A dog that comes when called because it knows that something great happens is more reliable than one that comes because it has to.
We regularly train the recall out of off-leash work as a genuine event: the dog comes, and the best we have to offer follows – play, food, effusive praise, a short romp. No half-hearted “good dog”.

Important: Never associate the recall with anything unpleasant – never use it directly for putting the dog on the leash and going straight home without playing first. Otherwise the dog learns: coming back means the end of freedom.
What we remember 🧠
Recognise the situation early – our own first reaction calm and immediate.
Consciously breathe out once – then recall calmly and clearly.
Leave the situation briskly and confidently – recall the dog all the way to the safe place and bring it into “sit” or “down”.
Assess the situation immediately and, if necessary, put the dog on the leash at once.
After the other party has gone, praise extensively and play.
Sources of error ⚠️
Reacting too late and communicating in an agitated or hectic way are the classic causes of failure.
Another mistake is breaking off the calling away too early and stopping too early – this does not take our dog far enough out of the situation.
Praising too early tempts our dog to project the emotions conveyed onto the other party that is still present.
Linking the recall exclusively with unwelcome consequences undermines the reliability of the recall in the long term.
Prerequisites and choice of dogs 🐕
Here we are speaking exclusively about the intended encounter of several socialised dogs off leash. All other states should be strictly avoided.

Criteria for a good choice of dogs: Socially compatible, familiar dogs without pronounced dominance or prey-drive trigger points, similar energy levels, positive previous experiences with each other. In case of doubt, it is better to decline once too often than to risk it once too often.
Unfamiliar dogs are first observed in neutral terrain and at a distance – only after a calm first encounter on the leash does the step to an off-leash encounter follow, if everything fits.
Training – movement as a group routine 🚶
What are we training? We consolidate the ability to instruct our dog into “down” with a calm, convincing voice in any situation of romping around – even while other dogs continue to run freely.

The principle of “movement instead of standing” as a group routine: Our many years of experience show that conflicts tend to arise where dog handlers and dogs stand in one place and the mood heats up for lack of room to move. If the dog handlers stay in motion, the potential for conflict drops significantly. NEVER STAND AROUND!
If confusing, emotional situations arise, all dog owners involved approach the dogs at the same time, briskly but silently, and each calmly and purposefully takes their own dog out of the situation.
Dog groups that have once been separated are not let run again in the same situation. Once separated, they stay separated for this meeting. (Exception: friendly dogs with a stable relationship.)
Follow-up – What to do after an escalating incident? 🔄

Immediately after the incident: dog on the leash, establish calm, leave the situation. No commenting afterwards, no scolding, no bringing in further arousal. The dog now needs stability from us – not an emotional working-through.
In the following days: deliberately step back to easier encounter situations. We rebuild trust in the sequence instead of immediately seeking the same stimulus level again.

Analysis from a calm distance: What was the trigger? Were we too close, too late, too agitated? Was the choice of dogs unsuitable? We answer these questions honestly and objectively – not to assign blame, but to be better prepared next time.
If a dog continues to react differently after an incident, brief advice from an experienced dog trainer or a vet is sensible.
What we remember 🧠
Assess conscientiously whether dogs can be let run together.
Stay calm in the case of minor disputes between the dogs.
Act quickly but calmly in heated situations.
Interrupt with “down” as long as no conflict is boiling up.
Separate wordlessly, directly and definitively as soon as there are confrontations.
Stay in motion – NEVER STAND AROUND!
Listen to your gut feeling – when dogs are romping around with each other, the human takes a back seat.
After an incident: step back, analyse, rebuild calmly.
Sources of error ⚠️
Classic source of error: unnecessary, prolonged standing around of the dog handlers in the group.
Addressing the dogs involved emotionally, handing out treats, joining in the play, bringing in toys and anything that could trigger jealous behaviour are strong triggers of conflict.
An unsuitable choice of dogs – dogs with incompatible characters or unfamiliar dogs without a calm first encounter – considerably increases the risk of escalation.
Immediately seeking the same stimulus level again after an incident, instead of deliberately stepping back and rebuilding.
What you should avoid as a matter of principle ⚠️
Avoid alarming behaviour of any kind.
Avoid stress and restlessness – in yourself first.
Avoid shortening the leash in stressful situations.
Avoid addressing loudly – neither the dog nor third parties.
Avoid going below your dog’s flight distance.
Avoid ending the alternative exercises too early.
Avoid praising too early while the situation is still ongoing.
Practical impulse: Breathe out once – then act

The most important moment in every conflict situation is the very first one. Before you give the first command: breathe out deeply once. This one breath separates reaction from action – and gives your dog the signal it needs: calm, not alarm. Practise this breath daily so that it comes automatically in an emergency.
→ Do I recognise my dog’s warning signals before the situation arises?
→ Do I actively and proactively look for the safe place – not only under pressure?
→ Do I keep the leash neutral and long enough in every phase of the encounter?
→ Do I train the recall regularly as a positive reward event?
→ Do I consciously breathe out before giving the first command in a stressful situation?
→ Do I train the off-leash recall step by step – from calm to urban?
→ Do I choose encounter dogs for running together deliberately and carefully?
→ Do I keep myself and the group in motion – NEVER STAND AROUND?
→ In case of escalation, do I separate wordlessly, directly and definitively – and then deliberately step back?
→ Do I always praise only after the situation has been completed fully and calmly – never too early!
